disguise: *** THE PAGE THAT COUNTS BEFORE IT HAS LOOKED ***
what it looked like: *** "Historical Record Search Results (0)" *** - complete, composed, confident, and indistinguishable from an empty result.
what it actually was: The heading rendering *** while the query was still running. *** Waiting returned the five records, then 210, then 822.
how it was caught: A control on *** Sancho Lerena ***, whose five records had been pulled twenty minutes earlier, returned zero as well. A known-false zero proves the fault is in the query.

disguise: *** AND IT IS STILL DOING IT SIX DAYS LATER ***
what it looked like: The same "(0)", three times in one sitting - on Justo, on Alfredo Justiniano, and on the first Gilberto sweep.
what it actually was: *** 39, 80 and 63 records. *** The heading is the page talking to itself before the results arrive.
how it was caught: Reading the page *** twice ***, which is in this archive's habits precisely because of the entry above, and still nearly produced three false nulls in one evening.

disguise: *** THE SESSION THAT LOGGED ITSELF OUT AND DID NOT SAY SO ***
what it looked like: Three searches returning zero results *** and no "No Results Found" line *** - which is normally this archive's proof that a search ran.
what it actually was: The FamilySearch session had *** silently expired *** and every request was being redirected to ident.familysearch.org, the sign-in page. It does not announce a logout, and the page that arrives is not obviously an error.
how it was caught: The control, *** and only the control: *** "Sancho Lerena", which had returned three Canelones baptisms, returned nothing.

disguise: *** THE QUOTA ERROR WEARING AN EMPTY SHELF ***
what it looked like: A Google Books API response reading *** totalItems: None. ***
what it actually was: *** An HTTP 429 *** - the quota refusing, not the shelf being bare.
how it was caught: The status code, which the body never mentioned.

disguise: *** THE BLOCK BEHIND AN EMPTY BODY ***
what it looked like: A zero-length response, no error, no message.
what it actually was: *** "Access Denied - Error 15, this request was blocked by our security service" *** - delivered as an empty body rather than as a refusal.
how it was caught: The same class of failure as the quota error: *** the service failing in a way that resembles success. *** Worse than an outage, because an outage announces itself.

disguise: *** THE ZERO DELIVERED ON THE WAY TO A BLOCK ***
what it looked like: A clean-looking zero from the Granada index, moments before Error 15 arrived.
what it actually was: A search already being refused. *** "A zero delivered immediately before a block is the least trustworthy zero there is." ***
how it was caught: The control - *** "Juan de Lerena y Aguilar", a phrase known to return a hit because it was read an hour before *** - never loaded at all.

disguise: *** THE THROTTLE THAT EMPTIES A PAGE ***
what it looked like: Four consecutive image transcripts returning *** length zero *** - which looks exactly like four blank pages in a register.
what it actually was: *** Rate limiting. *** Image 86, re-read after a forty-second pause, gave 2,970 characters. Image 22 had failed three times across two days and read clean at 3,451.
how it was caught: A zero is never allowed to count as a read. *** Eleven pages would otherwise have been silently certified as empty. ***

disguise: *** AND THE EMPTY PAGE THAT WAS NOT THE THROTTLE ***
what it looked like: Three more empty transcripts, identical in every visible way to the throttle above.
what it actually was: *** Images outside the volume altogether. *** The film holds 421 images and several volumes, not the 148 assumed.
how it was caught: *** The page TITLE. *** A throttled page still resolves to the volume's name; an image outside the volume resolves to something else. Without that check the three would have been logged "not read" forever and the volume never called finished.

disguise: *** THE QUERY THAT CANNOT REACH WHAT IS THERE ***
what it looked like: Two exact-surname searches returning zero *** with *** the "No Results Found" line present.
what it actually was: The indexed surname was a *** compound - "Lerena y Armenta" - *** which exact matching will not reach.
how it was caught: A control showed the same query shape could not retrieve a record *** known to be in the collection. A null from a query that cannot find what is there is not a null. ***

disguise: *** THE COUNT THAT HAS NO ZERO TO GIVE ***
what it looked like: The FamilySearch *** personas API *** answering 8,549 for surname Lerena in Uruguay.
what it actually was: *** The same 8,549 for every variant *** - add a given name, add a spouse, change the control's parameters entirely. The field ignores them. An invented surname, Zzzqqxx, still returns *** 102. ***
how it was caught: Running a control with *** deliberately different parameters *** and getting an identical number. No null can ever be drawn from an instrument that cannot return one.

disguise: *** THE COLLECTION FILED UNDER THE WRONG COUNTRY ***
what it looked like: A reel whose page title attributes it to *** COLOMBIA. ***
what it actually was: *** Uruguayan acts. *** The attribution is simply wrong on FamilySearch's side.
how it was caught: Reading the images rather than the label. *** Recorded because a researcher who trusted the page title would conclude the reel is Colombian and abandon it. ***

disguise: *** THE CORPUS THAT HOLDS THE WRONG RECORD TYPE ***
what it looked like: Spanish full-text searches for *** Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar *** returning zero.
what it actually was: The Andalusian full-text corpus holds *** nobility and notarial records, not parish registers. *** The zero meant "not findable by this instrument", not "not there".
how it was caught: Asking the control question - *** what Andalusian collections exist at all *** - instead of asking for the name again. Until the corpus is mapped, every Spanish null this archive produces is uninterpretable.

disguise: *** AND AGAIN THE NEXT DAY, ON A COUPLE WHOSE CHILDREN ARE IN THIS REGISTER ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** BERNABE LERENA and CASIMIRA PELAEZ ***, whose four children this archive has held since 13 September.
what it actually was: *** "(0)" ON THE FIRST READ AND 22 ON THE SECOND. *** Four seconds apart.
how it was caught: *** THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT IS THAT THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY KNOWN TO BE WRONG *** - the same thing that caught the very first one on 14 September. A control you happen to be standing on.

disguise: *** A PARENT'S SURNAME THAT REMOVES THE RECORDS IT MATCHES ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** AVELINO LERENA and CELEDONIA VILLADEMOROS ***, Uruguay - father's surname exact, mother's given name and surname supplied - returned a clean *** 0 ***, with rows rendered and the page settled. Read twice.
what it actually was: *** SEVEN RECORDS, AND TWO OF THEM ARE IN THIS REGISTER ALREADY *** - the christenings of Avelino Pedro Joaquin Silvestre in 1866 and Pedro Gualberto in 1870. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Celedonia' returned all seven. *** The likely mechanism: the mother's whole name sits unparsed in the given-name field, so supplying a surname excludes every record the parser failed on - and one of the seven displays its mother as 'Celedonia Villademoros', spelled exactly as asked.
how it was caught: *** THE ARCHIVE'S OWN RECORDS. *** The zero was known to be wrong before it was investigated, because this couple's children were entered on 20 September. *** No control would have caught it: *** the control for this shape - Alberto Lerena with Maria Ines Larriera - had returned sixteen records in the same session, which is what made the zero look trustworthy.

disguise: *** THE SAME TRAP AGAIN, ONE HOUR LATER, AND THIS TIME THE RULE CAUGHT IT ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on *** ALFREDO LERENA and HERMENEGILDA GAVARRO ***, Uruguay: *** 0 ***.
what it actually was: *** THREE RECORDS. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Hermenegilda' returned them - and they are her own death registration of 1940, which the archive had never seen. *** The index writes her surname 'Navarro de Terenadel', a machine mangling of GAVAZZO DE LERENA ***, so no spelling anybody would have guessed could have reached her.
how it was caught: *** BY THE RULE WRITTEN DOWN SIXTY MINUTES EARLIER: delete each added parameter in turn. *** The Villademoros zero cost an afternoon and was caught only because the archive already held the hidden records. This one cost one query. *** That is the whole argument for writing the rule down instead of remembering it. ***

disguise: *** THE ONE THAT PASSED EVERY TEST THIS ARCHIVE HAS ***
what it looked like: *** EVERY SEARCH RETURNING 0. *** Not a slow page and not an error: 'Historical Record Search Results (0)' with *** 'No Results Found' *** printed beneath it - the POSITIVE ASSERTION OF EMPTINESS this archive treats as the mark of a real null - *** stable across two reads twelve seconds apart, and still 0 after a NINETY-SECOND wait. ***
what it actually was: *** ONE BROWSER CONTEXT LOST ITS AUTH, AND ONLY ONE. *** First the arithmetic: *** surname GONZALEZ in URUGUAY returned 0 ***, in a collection running to millions, and the same URL that returned TEN records that morning returned 0 that afternoon. Then the apparent cause: full-text, asked the same question, *** REDIRECTED TO THE SIGN-IN PAGE ***. *** THAT LOOKED LIKE AN EXPIRED ACCOUNT AND WAS NOT. *** A sibling archive on the same machine ran both searches in the same minutes and got 3,652 and 3,967 with the account name in the nav bar. *** Each session's in-app browser is its own browser with its own cookie jar; one lost its auth and recovered by itself. *** In a FRESH TAB the same Gonzalez query returned *** 479,662 *** and Avelino with Ambrosia returned *** 10 *** again. *** THE RECORD SEARCH STILL NEVER SAID SO: it answered 0 with 'No Results Found' throughout, where full-text in the same context said plainly that it had no session. ***
how it was caught: *** BY A CONTROL WHOSE ANSWER CANNOT BE ZERO. *** Every other guard failed: the count was stable, the 'No Results Found' line was present, the wait was long, and a control run EARLIER THE SAME DAY had passed. *** THE ARCHIVE WAS ONE STEP FROM PUBLISHING A FABRICATED MECHANISM *** - that the parent-pair query cannot reach acts held only in full text - built entirely on this outage. *** SO THE RULE GAINS TWO WORDS: a control must be RECENT, and its answer must be ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO BE ZERO. *** *** AND A FREE TEST THAT COSTS ONE NAVIGATION: ask the FULL-TEXT search anything. It admits a lost session; the record search hides one behind a null. *** *** BUT THE REMEDY IS NOT WHAT THIS ARCHIVE FIRST SAID. *** It published that the account was signed out and that David would have to sign in again. *** Wrong, and corrected within the hour: open a new tab, or check another session's browser, before asking a person to do anything. *** The three nulls held over for re-testing - Luis with Carolina, Carlos with Luisa, Juan Arturo with Isidora - were all re-run against a live control and all three are still zero, so nothing was lost but the afternoon.

disguise: *** A PARENT-PAIR SEARCH THAT NEEDS A SURNAME AND WILL NOT SAY SO ***
what it looked like: *** SANCHO as father with MARIA as mother, Uruguay: 0. *** Read twice, with a live control - Gonzalez in Uruguay returning 479,660 minutes earlier.
what it actually was: *** THE QUERY SHAPE, NOT THE FAMILY. *** The arithmetic settles it without any judgement: *** father given name SANCHO alone returns 10,315. Mother given name MARIA alone returns 1,228,708. Together they return 0. *** Two fields matching five and seven figures cannot intersect at nothing in a country where Maria is the commonest name a mother has. *** ADD THE TWO SURNAMES - Llerena and Fernandez - AND THE SAME QUERY RETURNS SIX, every one of them real. ***
how it was caught: *** BY ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE ONLY GUARD THAT HAS NEVER FAILED HERE. *** The rule this yields is worth more than the instance: *** a parent-pair query with GIVEN NAMES ONLY returns zero whatever the truth is, so at least one parent SURNAME must be supplied before any null from this shape means anything. *** Every earlier zero in this archive drawn from given names alone is void; every one drawn with a surname stands.

disguise: *** THE NULL THAT MEANS 'NOT INDEXED', AND SAYS SO ***
what it looked like: Searched 27 September 2026 for the MARRIAGE of Alejandro M. Lerena and Elisa Villademoros, Uruguay - under LERENA and under *** SERENA ***, the spelling that had hidden the 1877 act naming his parents. Nothing. *** THE CONTROL WAS RUN IN THE SAME MINUTES AND IS THE RIGHT KIND: *** a MONTEVIDEO PARISH MARRIAGE OF THE SAME ERA that this archive already holds - Luis Lerena and Julia Juanico, 19 December 1864, San Francisco de Asis. It returns, and it returns WITH THE GROOM'S PARENTS ATTACHED. *** SO THE INSTRUMENT REACHES 1860s MONTEVIDEO MARRIAGES AND CARRIES PARENTS ON THEM ***, and the null is about THIS ACT rather than about the shelf. *** IT IS RECORDED AS 'NOT IN THE INDEXED CORPUS', NOT AS 'DID NOT HAPPEN' *** - the couple's eldest child was baptised in 1873, so a marriage exists. *** THIS IS THE FIRST ENTRY IN THIS FILE WHERE THE CONTROL WAS CHOSEN TO MATCH THE ERA, THE CITY AND THE RECORD TYPE *** rather than merely to be impossible-to-be-zero, and it is the better habit.
what it actually was: 27 September 2026

disguise: *** THE ZERO THAT IS PROBABLY TRUE, AND SAYS WHY ***
what it looked like: Trove, 27 September 2026. Every Lerena name returned ZERO in Australian newspapers. *** THAT IS NOT INTERESTING BY ITSELF *** - an Argentine-Uruguayan family need never appear in Australia, so the zero could mean anything. *** SO THE CONTROL WAS CHOSEN TO ASK THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS: COULD THIS CORPUS HAVE CARRIED HIM? *** Pablo Armando was a racehorse trainer at the Cape, and Australian papers covered South African racing from the 1890s onward - *** 11,500 hits ***, with headings like 'SOUTH AFRICAN RACING MATTERS - JOHANNESBURG RACING FEES'. *** THE SHELF IS FULL AND HE IS NOT ON IT. *** This entry is here because it is the OPPOSITE of the rest of the file: a null this archive believes, recorded with the work that earns the right to believe it. *** AND A SECOND LESSON: the only multi-term hits, 'Brayley Bideford', were PAGE-LEVEL ARTEFACTS - Trove indexes a whole Family Notices column as one article, and that one ran to 14,464 characters. ***
what it actually was: 27 September 2026

disguise: *** A PLACE FILTER THAT SILENTLY MATCHES NOTHING ***
what it looked like: FamilySearch's record search, asked for *** TAYLOR baptisms at Northam, Devon, father WILLIAM, 1869-1891 ***, returned *** 0 ***. Twice, read twice each. Loosening the father gave 0 as well.
what it actually was: *** THE PLACE PARAMETER WAS DOING NOTHING EXCEPT ZEROING THE RESULT. *** The control - *** surname TAYLOR at Northam, Devon, 1860-1900, with no other constraint at all *** - also returned 0, which is impossible for a parish of that size in a county whose censuses FamilySearch holds. *** AND THE OPPOSITE FAILURE IN THE SAME SESSION: *** the same search with `q.birthLikePlace=Devon, England` returned *** 6,941 *** results, from Kent, Northamptonshire, Wiltshire and Hampshire. *** The place field was ignored when it was loose and fatal when it was tight ***, and neither behaviour was visible from the result.
how it was caught: *** BY RUNNING THE CONTROL BEFORE BELIEVING THE NULL. *** One search with the family stripped out, and the zero fell over. This is the habit the file was written for.

disguise: *** A FULL-NAME SEARCH AGAINST AN INDEX THAT HOLDS INITIALS ***
what it looked like: *** 'Horace Archibald Taylor' *** on FamilySearch, no dates, no place: *** 0 results. *** Same for *** 'Mary Septima Taylor' *** and *** 'Agnes Walker Taylor' ***, all three of them people this archive has on records.
what it actually was: *** THE INDEX CARRIES THEM UNDER AN INITIAL. *** The 1891 census transcription reads *** 'Horace A' ***, and a given-name search for the full form matches nothing. *** THIS IS THE SAME TRAP THE ARCHIVE ALREADY RECORDED FOR THE GRO INDEX *** - the September note says Horace and William were each found only after dropping the second forename - *** and it was walked into again on a different site five days later. ***
how it was caught: *** BY TESTING A PERSON WHO CERTAINLY EXISTS. *** Three known people returning zero is a broken search, not three absent people.

disguise: *** A FIELD THAT LOOKS LIKE DATA AND IS A DEFAULT ***
what it looked like: South Africa's Transvaal and Orange Free State civil death indexes give *** 'Age: 0 days' *** for both of Roque Lerena's infant children - the boy who died at Bloemfontein on 22 May 1932 and *** ANTOINETTE SEPTIMA LYNETTE *** on 7 January 1943. Read literally, each was born on the day it died.
what it actually was: *** NEITHER CAN BE TRUE, AND THE PROOF IS THAT BOTH ARE WRONG THE SAME WAY. *** The family tree has the 1932 boy at *** five days *** and Antoinette at *** four ***. *** Two independent dates disagreeing with the index in the SAME DIRECTION is the signature of an unfilled field carrying a default ***, not of two coincidental errors. *** THE NEAR MISS: *** this archive was one step from publishing 'the tree says five days and the record says none, so the tree is wrong' - a correction built on a blank.
how it was caught: *** BY READING THE SECOND RECORD BEFORE WRITING UP THE FIRST. *** One '0 days' is a fact; two in a row, against two different trees, is a form field.

disguise: *** A SEARCH TOOL THAT ERRORS, READ AS A CORPUS THAT IS EMPTY ***
what it looked like: FamilySearch's full-text search, given a South African place in the URL, returns *** 'Something Went Wrong - unfortunately, something went wrong, and we are unable to display the search results.' *** Unfiltered searches surfaced no South African collection either, and this archive published that *** South Africa is not in the corpus ***.
what it actually was: *** IT IS IN THE CORPUS. *** The URL parameter is broken; *** the PLACE FACET inside the page works perfectly ***, and the surname returns seven hits across four South African collections - including a voters' roll entry for *** ROQUE LUIS ARMANDO LERENA *** and a land record carrying *** NUNO FERNANDO LERENA's exact birth date ***. The unfiltered searches hid them because 1,985 results ranked Peru and Spain above seven South African ones.
how it was caught: *** BY OPENING THE FILTER IN THE PAGE INSTEAD OF WRITING IT INTO THE URL. *** The lesson is one word longer than the one this archive already had: *** run the control before believing the null - and when a tool ERRORS rather than returns nothing, that is not a null at all. *** *** CONFIRMED AGAIN 9 October 2026, AND IT IS NOT A SOUTH AFRICA PROBLEM. *** The identical 'Something Went Wrong' came back for *** f.recordCountry=Uruguay ***, a country this archive searches daily and whose records it had already read that morning. *** SO THE BROKEN THING IS THE PARAMETER, NOT THE COUNTRY *** - which is the stronger statement, and the one worth carrying: *** never put a place in a full-text URL; open the facet. ***

disguise: *** A RECORD PAGE THAT TIMES OUT AND LOOKS LIKE A RECORD WITH NOTHING IN IT ***
what it looked like: A FamilySearch full-text image page, opened straight from a result list, rendered its title and then *** 'Unable to load the data - loading record data is taking longer than expected. Please try again later.' *** Read for content at that moment it returns a page with *** ZERO occurrences of the surname *** - a clean, quiet, entirely false null.
what it actually was: *** A TRANSIENT LOAD FAILURE. *** The record was intact. A single click of its own REFRESH button returned the full image, the names panel and the AI transcript - *** which contained the baptism that answered the 1894 dispensation ***, naming Juan Lerena's parents as Bernabe and Casimira Pelaez. *** THE PAGE THAT APPEARED TO HOLD NOTHING HELD THE FIND OF THE DAY. ***
how it was caught: *** BY READING THE PAGE'S OWN ERROR TEXT INSTEAD OF COUNTING ITS HITS. *** The search for the surname returned 0 and the page said why, one line above. This is the same rule as the row before it - *** a tool that ERRORS is not a corpus that is EMPTY *** - but one level lower: *** not the search, the single record ***. *** THE PRACTICAL FORM: BEFORE RECORDING A NULL ON A RECORD PAGE, CHECK THAT THE RECORD LOADED. ***

disguise: *** A SIGNED-OUT SEARCH, MISREAD AS A FACT ABOUT HOW AN INDEX IS SHAPED ***
what it looked like: The FamilySearch record search returned a clean, confident *** 0 Results *** for *** q.fatherGivenName=Carlos & q.fatherSurname=Lerena & q.motherSurname=Carniglia *** - and again for the same pair without the given name. A null for a couple, stated plainly by the search, with no error and no throttle.
what it actually was: *** THE SESSION HAD SILENTLY SIGNED OUT, AND A SIGNED-OUT SEARCH RETURNS A RESTRICTED TIER. *** This row first said the zero proved that a PARENT-pair query cannot reach records indexed with the FATHER as principal. *** THAT WAS A THEORY BUILT ON A LOGGED-OUT SESSION. *** The same spouse-pair query that had returned three true hits an hour earlier - and from which two acts were read off the plate - returned twenty-one rows of United States census and *** NOT ONE CARRYING THE NAME ***. The page said so at the top: 'Create a free account or sign in to see all available results.'
how it was caught: *** BY RE-RUNNING THE CONTROL AFTER THE NULL INSTEAD OF ONLY BEFORE IT. *** *** THE RULE THIS COST: A CONTROL RUN BEFORE A NULL PROVES NOTHING ABOUT THE NULL IF THE SERVICE CAN CHANGE STATE IN BETWEEN. *** On any signed-in service, the control must be re-run AFTER the null it is protecting. *** AND THE CHEAPEST POSSIBLE DETECTOR WAS ON THE PAGE ALL ALONG: *** the account name in the header, or the words 'sign in to see all available results'. *** CHECK THE HEADER BEFORE BELIEVING THE RESULTS. ***

disguise: *** TWENTY-ONE ROWS OF NOISE THAT LOOK LIKE RESULTS - AND THE CAUSE WAS NOT WHAT THIS ROW FIRST SAID ***
what it looked like: *** q.surname=Lerena & q.spouseSurname=Llanos *** returned a full page of results - twenty-one rows - and *** q.givenName=Salvador & q.surname=Lorena~ *** returned twenty-one more. A reader skimming either would say the search found things.
what it actually was: *** NOT ONE ROW CARRIED THE CONSTRAINT *** - every hit was United States census or New Zealand passenger data: Llorens, Lorraine, Lohren, Lorene, Lorino. *** THIS ROW FIRST BLAMED A FALLBACK: *** that the service silently widens a filtered search when it matches nothing. *** THE REAL CAUSE WAS A SIGNED-OUT SESSION ***, which returns the same restricted fuzzy tier for every query whatever the constraint - and the page says so in one line above the results. *** THE OBSERVATION WAS RIGHT AND THE EXPLANATION WAS WRONG ***, which is worth more here than either on its own.
how it was caught: *** BY CHECKING WHETHER ANY RETURNED ROW ACTUALLY CONTAINED THE CONSTRAINING TERM ***, which is still the right first move and still catches it. *** BUT THE SECOND MOVE IS THE ONE THAT NAMES THE CAUSE: READ THE HEADER. *** A page offering to let you 'sign in to see all available results' is not a corpus and not a fallback - it is a logged-out session. *** COUNT THE ROWS THAT MATCH WHAT YOU ASKED FOR, THEN ASK WHO THE SERVICE THINKS YOU ARE. ***

disguise: *** A COMPOUND-SURNAME SEARCH THAT MATCHES TWO DIFFERENT PEOPLE WHO SIGNED THE SAME PAGE ***
what it looked like: The phrase *** 'Lerena Cardozo' *** returned two Durazno birth registers of 1915, which looked like children of the *** 1911 LERENA-CARDOZO DISPENSATION COUPLE *** - exactly the thing being searched for, in exactly the right years.
what it actually was: *** NEITHER ACT IS ABOUT A LERENA AT ALL. *** The phrase matched because *** PEDRO S. LERENA *** signed at the request of an illiterate declarant and *** SATURNINO CARDOZO *** witnessed the same act, so the two surnames fall adjacent in the signature block. *** A COMPOUND SEARCH CANNOT TELL A PERSON'S TWO SURNAMES FROM TWO PEOPLE'S ONE SURNAME EACH. ***
how it was caught: *** BY READING THE ACT INSTEAD OF THE HIT. *** *** THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HELD THE SAME TRAP IN ANOTHER SERVICE: *** Trove treats a whole FAMILY NOTICES COLUMN as one article, so 'Brayley Bideford' matched two terms set in the same column of type. *** IT IS THE SAME ERROR IN A NEW PLACE - PROXIMITY READ AS RELATIONSHIP *** - and the compound technique, which has been this archive's sharpest tool for a month, has this as its specific failure mode. *** THE TELL IS CHEAP: IF THE TWO SURNAMES APPEAR IN A LIST OF SIGNATURES RATHER THAN IN A PERSON'S NAME, IT IS NOT A COMPOUND. *** And the accident was not wasted: it found a literate Lerena at Tejera nobody had looked for.

disguise: *** THE SAME SIGN-OUT, BUT THIS TIME IT ONLY TOOK THE IMAGES ***
what it looked like: *** AN INDEX RECORD THAT READ PERFECTLY, AND AN IMAGE VIEWER THAT DID NOT. *** The record page for ark 1:1:6LXZ-JV32 loaded in full - names, ages, certificate number, parents, even the SAVE and EDIT controls that only appear to a signed-in user - and a check for the "Create a free account" line came back clean. *** EVERY SIGN SAID THE SESSION WAS LIVE. *** Then following that record's own VIEW ORIGINAL DOCUMENT link landed on ident.familysearch.org.
what it actually was: *** A PARTIAL SIGN-OUT, WHICH IS MORE DANGEROUS THAN A WHOLE ONE. *** The indexed text of this collection is served to anyone; the IMAGES are not. So a session can read records all day, pass its own sign-in control, and still be unable to open a single plate - and if it had been looking for a NULL rather than an image it would have had no warning at all. *** THE LESSON IS THAT "AM I SIGNED IN?" IS NOT ONE QUESTION. *** It has to be asked of the thing actually being used, and an index page cannot answer it for an image viewer.
how it was caught: *** BY TRYING TO READ A PLATE AND WATCHING THE URL. *** Nothing clever: the DeepZoom step was about to run when the page title came back as "Sign-in to your account". Because this archive had already been burned by disguise seventeen it stopped rather than retried, recorded both plates as UNREAD RATHER THAN EMPTY, and drew no conclusion from the failure - which is the whole point of having a taxonomy of these. *** AND IT WAS LIFTED THE SAME DAY: *** the owner signed the session in and both plates were read within the hour. *** THE BLOCK IS KEPT ON THE BOOKS ANYWAY ***, because the disguise is what is worth remembering - not the inconvenience, which lasted ninety minutes, but the fact that every test this archive runs for 'am I signed in?' returned TRUE while the images were shut. *** AND THE OTHER SHAPE APPEARED THE SAME DAY, WHICH IS WHY THIS ROW NOW DESCRIBES TWO. *** Hours later the session was signed out *** COMPLETELY ***: the image ark redirected, and so did the FULL-TEXT SEARCH, which had worked an hour before. *** THE FULL SIGN-OUT ANNOUNCES ITSELF AND IS HARMLESS; THE PARTIAL ONE DOES NOT AND IS NOT. *** A session that can still search will happily record zeros; a session that cannot search knows immediately. *** SO THE CHECK IS NOT 'AM I SIGNED IN' BUT 'DOES THE THING I AM ABOUT TO USE STILL ANSWER' ***, run against the instrument itself and run AFTER the result, not before.

disguise: *** THE BRIDE WHO WAS THE GROOM'S MOTHER - AN INDEX THAT INVENTS A PARTY BY COPYING ONE ***
what it looked like: A clean parish-index search row: *** "Socorro Lerena, Bride, Marriage 15 July 1885, Santisima Trinidad, Spouses Serapio Fernandez" ***. Name, role, date, place and spouse, all present, nothing missing and nothing obviously mangled. *** IT LOOKS LIKE A SOURCED MARRIAGE AND IT WAS WRITTEN INTO THE REGISTER AS ONE. ***
what it actually was: *** THE GROOM'S MOTHER PUT IN THE BRIDE'S PLACE BY A COMPUTER INDEXER. *** Socorro Lerena was born about 1832 and was a widow with a grown son in 1885 - that son being the Serapio Fernandez of this very act. The real bride was ANTONINA LERENA, dispensed three weeks earlier. *** THE INDEX HAD NO BRIDE, SO IT TOOK THE ONLY OTHER LERENA ON THE PAGE AND GAVE HER THE GROOM'S DETAILS. ***
how it was caught: *** BY OPENING THE RECORD AND NOTICING THE TWO PARTIES WERE IDENTICAL. *** The bride is given age thirty, born 1855, born at Santisima Trinidad, resident at Santisima Trinidad, soltera - and the groom is given age thirty, born 1855, born at Santisima Trinidad, resident at Santisima Trinidad, soltero. *** EVERY FIELD THE SAME. *** A real couple almost never matches on all five. *** THE RULE: WHEN BOTH PARTIES TO AN INDEXED MARRIAGE SHARE EVERY ATTRIBUTE, ONE OF THEM HAS BEEN MANUFACTURED FROM THE OTHER *** - and the clue to WHO was manufactured is which of them already had a different age on another record.

disguise: *** A NULL IN ONE FAMILYSEARCH INDEX IS NOT A NULL IN FAMILYSEARCH ***
what it looked like: Three of this archive's standing conclusions: that the marriage of Alejandro M. Lerena and Elisa Villademoros "is not in the indexed corpus and must be walked by image"; that Jose Loreto Lerena "is not in FamilySearch's indexed Uruguayan records after his own baptism"; and that Sancho Llerena appears "never as the principal" across 401 results. *** EACH WAS A PROPERLY CONTROLLED NULL, WITH THE CONTROL RUN AND PASSED, AND EACH WAS STATED AS A FACT ABOUT FAMILYSEARCH. ***
what it actually was: *** THEY WERE FACTS ABOUT ONE OF ITS TWO INDEXES. *** The RECORD INDEX is built by transcribing entries into fields, so it catalogues principals and parents and loses everyone else on the page. The FULL-TEXT CORPUS is built by reading the page image, so it finds a name anywhere - in a margin, in a witness list, inside a deposition. *** THE 1871 MARRIAGE WAS IN THE SECOND ALL ALONG, FOUND BY ONE PHRASE SEARCH, after this archive had twice sentenced itself to an image walk. *** And Sancho Llerena, who the record index said was never a principal, turns up giving sworn testimony in his own voice.
how it was caught: *** BY FINDING A MARRIAGE THAT HAD BEEN DECLARED UNFINDABLE, AND THEN ASKING WHAT ELSE HAD BEEN DECLARED ON THE SAME BASIS. *** Four work-list rows were found reasoning from an index null; two were re-tested the same hour. One produced a new record of the archive's apex ancestor. The other, Jose Loreto, came back null in BOTH instruments - with the control run AFTER the null - which makes that row's conclusion far stronger than it was. *** THE RULE: BEFORE WRITING "NOT IN THE INDEXED CORPUS", NAME WHICH INDEX. ***

disguise: *** A FALSE POSITIVE INSTEAD OF A FALSE ZERO - the first in this file, and it inflates a search rather than emptying one. ***
what it looked like: *** 700 full-text hits for LERENA in Argentina ***, overwhelmingly Buenos Aires probate files, read as 700 appearances of a rare surname in one province.
what it actually was: *** THE SPANISH WORD FOR 'INHERITANCE' IS HERENCIA, AND THE TRANSCRIBER READS IT AS 'LERENA'. *** In the 1795 Convento de San Francisco file the transcript gives *** 'admitio absolutamente LA LERENA' *** and *** 'verificarse LA LERENCIA' ***. The legal Spanish is 'admitir la herencia' - to accept an inheritance - and 'la lerena' means nothing at all. *** SO IN A CORPUS MADE ENTIRELY OF PROBATE FILES, THE COMMONEST WORD IN THE CORPUS IMPERSONATES THE SURNAME THIS ARCHIVE SEARCHES FOR. *** The same page produced 'non lerena rece en el' and 'as lerena le coma con la tras' - both of them herencia, neither of them a person. *** THIS IS WHY A RESULT COUNT IS NOT A FINDING: *** the honest size of that result set is unknown and much smaller than 700, and every hit has to be read before it is counted.
how it was caught: *** BY OPENING A HIT THAT LOOKED PROMISING FOR A DIFFERENT REASON. *** The 1795 file was opened because it is from Ramon Lerena's decade, not because the snippet looked wrong. Reading the sentence around the word - rather than the word - showed it was a noun, not a name. *** THE GENERAL RULE IT GIVES: in a full-text corpus, check what your surname is a MISREADING OF in the language and the document type you are searching. *** A surname that collides with an ordinary word of the register's own vocabulary will be found everywhere and mean nothing.

disguise: *** AN INDEX THAT MUST OUTPUT A MOTHER WILL BUILD ONE OUT OF THE FATHER'S SURNAME - and it did it twice in one morning. ***
what it looked like: Two Uruguayan *** LERENA-MARRIED-A-LERENA couples ***, returned by an exact-surname parent-pair query and entered here as couples: ALEJANDRO LERENA with BARBARA LERENA at San Jose de Mayo in 1846, and VITALIANO LERENA with ANDREA LERENA at Trinidad in 1906.
what it actually was: *** NEITHER WOMAN WAS A LERENA, AND ONE OF THEM WAS NOT A WIFE. *** The 1846 act reads *** 'hijo natural de BARBARA, ESCLAVA DE D.n ALEJANDRO LERENA' *** - an enslaved woman, given the surname of the man who held her, and promoted to his spouse by the indexer. The 1906 act reads *** 'hija legitima de Don VITALIANO LERENA y de Dona ANDREA ETCHEBERSE' ***, with ETCHEBERSE broken across the page opening - and the index took the father's surname and gave it to her. *** THE MECHANISM IS THE SAME BOTH TIMES: the schema has a MOTHER field, the act does not fill it the way the schema expects, and the surname nearest to hand gets used. *** *** SO A PARENT-PAIR QUERY CANNOT TELL A MARRIAGE FROM A SLAVE-HOLDING, OR A MOTHER FROM A LINE BREAK. ***
how it was caught: *** BY OPENING THE ACTS, FIRST THING, BECAUSE AN INDEX ENTRY CONTRADICTED SOMEBODY THIS ARCHIVE THOUGHT IT KNEW. *** The four couples were entered index-level with every row saying so, and the first two opened both collapsed. *** THE RULE THIS GIVES: a parent pair in an index is a CLAIM ABOUT A SCHEMA, not a claim about a marriage - and where both parents share a surname it is MORE suspect, not less, because that is exactly the shape the failure produces. ***

disguise: *** THE COUNT THAT COUNTED THE WHOLE INDEX ***
what it looked like: A parent-pair query on the FamilySearch personas API returning *** 3,405 *** couples where the web page, on the identical parameters, showed 38. A big number looks like a find, so this one does not disguise a zero - it disguises a NULL by burying it.
what it actually was: *** THE API RANKS BY DEFAULT AND FILTERS ONLY ON REQUEST. *** Without `m.queryRequireDefault=on` every q.* parameter is a RELEVANCE BOOST, not a condition, so the response returns the whole searchable index sorted by how well it matches. The web UI sends that parameter on every search; a hand-built URL does not.
how it was caught: *** THE CONTROL WAS DESIGNED TO FAIL AND DID. *** Father Sancho Lerena + mother Maria Fernandez - a couple with exactly five known records - came back *** 17,448,030. *** A control is only useful when you know what number it must NOT return. Replaying the UI's own request through the network log showed the missing parameter; with it, the same two queries return 3 and 39.

disguise: *** THE INDEX THAT MOVED HIM 1,400 KM ***
what it looked like: Pablo Armando's own enrolment card is indexed by FamilySearch with birthplace *** "Rosario de Lerma, Salta, Argentina" *** - so any search filtered to Rosario, SANTA FE returns nothing for the one man this archive is built on.
what it actually was: *** A GEOCODING ERROR IN THE INDEX, NOT A READING OF THE CARD. *** The card is printed `Nacido en` and filled in by hand *** "Rosario de Santa Fe" *** - unambiguous, and transcribed in data/enrolment-card-1908.tsv on 10 September. The indexer resolved the bare word "Rosario" to the wrong one of Argentina's two.
how it was caught: Found 12 October while reading the API rows behind a variant sweep - the record came back under a query with no place filter at all, and the place it carried was wrong. *** Any place-filtered null at Rosario de Santa Fe is now suspect for this reason alone. ***

disguise: *** THE NULL THAT WAS TRUE OF THE QUERY SHAPE ***
what it looked like: A signed-in, properly controlled spouse-pair search returning *** exactly one record for a couple *** - the constraint binding, eleven rows of the rare surname coming back across five countries, and only one of them theirs.
what it actually was: *** A QUERY THAT CANNOT REACH THE RECORD TYPE THE ANSWER IS IN. *** q.surname + q.spouseSurname constrains on a MARRIAGE RELATIONSHIP. A census has none - it is a list of people in a dwelling, each indexed separately - so no census can ever satisfy a spouse-pair query, however well it binds. The couple were on the 1895 Buenos Aires census the whole time.
how it was caught: *** By opening the census sheet for an unrelated reason two days later. *** Every earlier disguise in this file is a search that FAILED and looked like an answer; this one is a search that WORKED and still produced a false null. *** The control proves the query is running. It cannot prove the query can see the record. ***

disguise: *** THE PLACE FILTER THAT QUIETLY WIDENS TO THE COUNTRY ***
what it looked like: A departmental place filter returning a plausible, specific number - 208 for Artigas against 699 for Flores and 891 for Montevideo - with a control at Osaka returning a clean 0.
what it actually was: *** A PARSER THAT FALLS BACK TO THE COUNTRY WHEN THE SUB-PLACE DOES NOT RESOLVE, AND AN INDEX FULL OF PLACE-LESS ROWS. *** q.anyPlace='Nonesuch, Uruguay' returns 1,787 - the whole-country count - so an unresolvable department silently becomes 'Uruguay'; and records indexed only to 'Uruguay' satisfy every departmental query. 57 of the first hundred Artigas hits carry no place at all.
how it was caught: *** By opening one of the returned records, which turned out to be a Montevideo death. *** The Osaka control proved the filter binds on COUNTRY and was read as proving it binds on DEPARTMENT. *** The useful control would have been a department that does not exist - and it takes one query. ***

disguise: *** THE ABBREVIATION THAT BROKE A PHRASE SEARCH ***
what it looked like: *** 'esclava de D.n Alejandro Lerena' *** - a phrase this archive has READ, word for word, off a plate - returning *** No Results Found *** in full text. A clean, composed empty result on a phrase known to exist.
what it actually was: *** THE ABBREVIATION. *** The same search as *** 'esclava de Alejandro Lerena' *** returns the two documents at once - the baptism and the burial. The rule is exact, and was pinned down the same hour by writing the phrase three ways: *** 'esclava de D.n Alejandro Lerena' matches NOTHING; 'esclava de Don Alejandro Lerena' matches; 'esclava de Alejandro Lerena' matches. *** So the search tolerates a MISSING word and chokes on an ABBREVIATED one.
how it was caught: *** By running the known phrase as a CONTROL before trusting two nulls built on the same shape. *** Those two - 'esclava de Don Pedro Lerena' and 'liberta de Don Pedro Lerena' - were about to be recorded. *** A phrase search is only as good as the transcriber's abbreviations, and this archive's sources are full of D.n, D.a, S.n and V.a. ***
